title: System Architecture Concepts
objective: Study-guide review — CISSP — Domain 3: Security Architecture and Engineering: System Architecture Concepts.

items: Ring 0 (Kernel mode) — Most privileged; OS kernel
Ring 1 — Operating system services
Ring 2 — Drivers and protocols
Ring 3 (User mode) — Least privileged; applications
Supervisor state — CPU in Ring 0; full hardware access

blocks.text: The protection ring model enforces privilege separation:

items: User applications (Ring 3) cannot directly access hardware
System calls mediate access from user mode to kernel mode
Hardware enforces the boundaries between rings
Malware in Ring 3 is contained by ring boundaries (in theory)

blocks.title: Exam trap
blocks.text: ⚠️ Exam Trap: Most modern operating systems only use Ring 0 (kernel) and Ring 3 (user). Rings 1 and 2 are typically unused. Hypervisors sometimes operate at Ring -1 (below the kernel).

items: Process isolation — Each process has its own memory space
Hardware segmentation — CPU enforces memory boundaries
Virtual memory — Abstracts physical memory; provides isolation
ASLR (Address Space Layout Randomization) — Randomizes memory addresses
DEP (Data Execution Prevention) — Prevents code execution in data segments
One process from accessing another process's memory
Buffer overflow attacks (with DEP, ASLR, stack canaries)
Unauthorized access to kernel memory from user space

blocks.text: From Stewart: "Controlling who may access data stored in memory while a computer is in use is primarily the responsibility of the operating system."

items: Hypervisor — Software that creates and manages virtual machines
Type 1 (Bare-metal) — Runs directly on hardware (VMware ESXi, Hyper-V)
Type 2 (Hosted) — Runs on top of an OS (VirtualBox, VMware Workstation)
VM Escape — Attacker breaks out of VM to access hypervisor or other VMs
VM Sprawl — Uncontrolled proliferation of VMs creating management challenges

blocks.text: From the Official CBK: "There is always the possibility that unpatched defects in the hardware or hypervisor might be known to a threat actor who is then able to compromise the protections that are supposed to prevent unrelated clients..." Key virtualization security concerns:

items: VM Escape — Most critical threat; allows access to hypervisor
Inter-VM attacks — VMs on same host attacking each other
Side-channel attacks — Extracting data from shared CPU/cache (Spectre, Meltdown)
Snapshot security — VM snapshots may contain sensitive data in memory
Resource contention — One VM consuming resources affects others (DoS)

blocks.title: Exam trap
blocks.text: ⚠️ Exam Trap: Type 1 hypervisors are MORE secure than Type 2 because they don't depend on an underlying OS (smaller attack surface).

items: IaaS — Customer controls OS and applications; provider controls infrastructure
PaaS — Customer controls applications; provider controls OS and below
SaaS — Provider controls everything; customer only uses the application
Shared Responsibility Model — Security responsibility divided between provider and customer
More abstraction = less customer control, more provider responsibility
Public Cloud — Shared infrastructure, multi-tenant
Private Cloud — Dedicated infrastructure, single tenant
Hybrid Cloud — Mix of public and private
Community Cloud — Shared among organizations with common interests

blocks.text: From Stewart: "Cloud computing is a concept where processing and storage are performed elsewhere over a network connection rather than locally." ⚠️ Exam Trap: In ALL cloud models, the CUSTOMER is always responsible for their DATA. You can outsource operations but never accountability.

items: TPM — Hardware chip that stores cryptographic keys securely
Provides hardware-based root of trust
Supports measured boot — validates boot integrity
Used for BitLocker, full-disk encryption key storage
Resistant to software attacks because keys never leave the chip
